title: 1 Samuel 24:8–15
context: David follows Saul out of the cave, bows to him, and shows the piece of robe as proof that he had the chance to kill him and refused. He appeals to the LORD as judge and calls himself no threat to the king, no more than a dead dog or a flea.

verses.text: David also arose afterward, and went out of the cave and cried after Saul, saying, “My lord the king!” When Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth, and showed respect.
verses.arminianNotes: David follows Saul out of the cave, calls him my lord the king, and bows to the ground. Arminian readers see humility and respect offered freely to the man who is trying to kill him, an example of loving one’s enemy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David honors Saul’s office publicly, at great personal risk. By stepping into the open, he entrusts his safety to God rather than to the darkness of the cave.

verses.text: David said to Saul, “Why do you listen to men’s words, saying, ‘Behold, David seeks to harm you’?
verses.arminianNotes: David asks why Saul listens to men who say David seeks his harm. Arminian readers note the appeal to Saul’s reason and to his responsibility to weigh what he hears rather than follow rumor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David naming the slanderers around Saul while still holding the king accountable for heeding them. Sin is often fed by voices a person chooses to believe.

verses.text: Behold, today your eyes have seen how the LORD had delivered you today into my hand in the cave. Some urged me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, ‘I will not stretch out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD’s anointed.’
verses.arminianNotes: David says the LORD delivered Saul into his hand that day, and some urged him to kill Saul, but he spared him. Arminian readers see a genuine moral choice, made freely out of reverence for God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David reads the opportunity as a test rather than a license. Providence places Saul in his power, but God’s command not to harm the anointed governs what David does with it.

verses.text: Moreover, my father, behold, yes, see the skirt of your robe in my hand; for in that I cut off the skirt of your robe and didn’t kill you, know and see that there is neither evil nor disobedience in my hand. I have not sinned against you, though you hunt for my life to take it.
verses.arminianNotes: David holds up the piece of the robe and calls Saul my father. Arminian readers see evidence offered to persuade Saul and an open hand extended toward reconciliation, which Saul remains free to accept or refuse.
verses.reformedNotes: Saul was David’s father-in-law (18:27), so the address is both affectionate and pointed. Reformed readers note how the robe proves David’s innocence: neither evil nor disobedience is in his hand.

verses.text: May the LORD judge between me and you, and may the LORD avenge me of you; but my hand will not be on you.
verses.arminianNotes: David asks the LORD to judge between them and avenge him, but insists his own hand will not touch Saul. Arminian readers see trust in God’s justice replacing the desire for personal revenge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers connect this with the principle that vengeance belongs to God (Deuteronomy 32:35, cited in Romans 12:19). David hands the case to the divine judge and refuses to act as his own avenger.

verses.text: As the proverb of the ancients says, ‘Out of the wicked comes wickedness;’ but my hand will not be on you.
verses.arminianNotes: David quotes a proverb of the ancients: out of the wicked comes wickedness. Arminian readers take his point that conduct reveals character; if he were wicked, he would have acted wickedly in the cave.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the proverb as an appeal to the fruit of the heart, much like the teaching that a tree is known by its fruit (Matthew 12:33). David’s restraint proves he is not the evildoer Saul imagines.

verses.text: Against whom has the king of Israel come out? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog? A flea?
verses.arminianNotes: David asks whom the king of Israel is pursuing: a dead dog, a flea? Arminian readers see humility and a plea for Saul to recognize how absurd and wasteful his chase has become.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note David’s self-abasement as a refusal to present himself as a rival for the throne. He uses similar language when he spares Saul a second time (26:20).

verses.text: May the LORD therefore be judge, and give sentence between me and you, and see, and plead my cause, and deliver me out of your hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: David closes by calling on the LORD to give sentence, plead his cause, and deliver him. Arminian readers see a man who has freely chosen to rest his case with God rather than secure it by force.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David entrusting himself to God as both judge and advocate, a pattern Christ later fulfills when he entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).
